# Symbolic Engineering

> Symbolic Engineering builds Contour, which predicts equipment failures from the plant data a company already holds. Contour reads process historians, SAP HANA and SAP PM, SCADA and maintenance systems, maps every sensor to the equipment and variable it measures, and builds reliability and failure models for each asset. The result is maintenance planned on the condition of the equipment, with every date traced to the records behind it.

Most plants already record what a reliability study needs. The equipment master and failure history sit in SAP, the process signals in a historian, the alarms in SCADA. They were never joined, so the analysis is assembled by hand, one asset at a time, and the maintenance calendar comes from the manufacturer's manual instead. Contour does the joining: it extracts the asset tree, links each asset to its history and instruments, describes how assets depend on each other in series and in parallel, and fits statistical and machine-learning models over that structure.

The approach has two halves. The plant is first described symbolically, as explicit structure: assets, components, variables, and the series and parallel dependencies between them. Reliability statistics and per-asset models are then fitted over that description, so a prediction knows which asset it is about and what fails with it. Reliability and maintenance is where Contour goes deepest; the same platform also serves funds and hospitals, wherever records exist and their meaning has never been written down.

Company: Symbolic Engineering. Product: Contour.
Operating regions: Europe, North America, Brazil.
Contact: contact@symbolic.engineering

## Components

Contour is a set of components that each do one job and share one model of the plant. They are described separately because each answers a different question; in an engagement they are deployed together.

- Integrate: Source Connectors (read-only replication from historians, SAP HANA/PM, SCADA and maintenance systems; nothing is written back); Asset Extraction (derives the asset hierarchy from functional locations, the equipment master and bills of materials, for engineers to confirm).
- Describe: Asset Tree (site, area, system, equipment and component, each node linked to failures, work orders, sensors and documents); Component Catalogue (maps each make and model to its failure modes and the variables that reveal them); Model Context Layer (maps every tag and field onto the asset and model variable it represents); [Reliability Block Diagrams](https://symbolic.engineering/product/reliability-block-diagrams/) (series, parallel, k-out-of-n and standby structure, including elements redundant paths share); Structure Rules (declarative rules that derive the block diagrams from the asset tree and process topology and keep them current); Failure Propagation (traces a component failure through the block diagrams to the function and production it takes down).
- Estimate: Reliability Indicators (MTBF, MTTF, MTTR and availability, recalculated on a schedule); Life Data Analysis (Weibull and related lifetime fits that treat units still in service as censored observations); System Reliability (combines component estimates over the block diagrams into system, line or plant reliability).
- Learn: Model Training (a model per asset on its own sensor history and failure record); Model Selection (automatic comparison of model families, kept on record); Model Operations (deployment, versioning and retraining); Model Monitoring (accuracy, input drift, anomalies and failure predictions).
- Serve: Agent Interface (exposes the plant model to AI assistants over the Model Context Protocol as typed, tested operations rather than generated queries); Lineage & Provenance (every figure carries the steps that produced it and the records it was built from).

Outputs are results of the components rather than components: failure prediction per asset, anomaly events, a predictive maintenance schedule, criticality ranking, and spares and outage planning.

## What Contour is not

Contour is not a rule engine. Structure Rules are declarative: they state what the structure of the plant is, for example that two pumps on one header with a duty and a standby designation form a one-out-of-two block, and Contour derives the block diagrams from them. Nothing fires. A rule engine holds conditions and actions and reacts when incoming facts match; Contour holds a description of the plant and answers questions asked of it. Contour answers only what the model describes, and a question outside it returns a refusal rather than an inference. It reads from the client's historian, ERP and maintenance systems and does not replace them.

## Use cases

- **Manufacturing and process industry** (lead case): the line is instrumented end to end and the maintenance system holds years of work orders, yet service intervals come from the calendar, the manufacturer's manual or the last shutdown, and reliability engineering is done by hand one asset at a time. Contour replicates the equipment master, failure history, process signals and alarm record, proposes the asset tree, attaches every instrument to the equipment and variable it measures, records what runs in series and what is redundant, estimates each asset's probability of failure, and states what that means for the line. The result is a maintenance window for each asset with the probability behind the date and the records it was built from.
- **Investment firms**: a fund with a data warehouse and capable DBAs still takes days to answer the questions that matter, and an AI assistant pointed at the warehouse is fluent, confident and wrong. Contour resolves the sources into a model carrying the firm's own vocabulary, queried through the agent interface, with lineage and provenance on every figure.
- **Hospitals and clinical engineering**: planned maintenance comes from manufacturers' intervals and says what is due, not which failure closes a theatre. Contour builds the dependency structure of the estate from the equipment register, the building management system and the service history, and orders planned work by what it protects. No patient data is required.

## Key definitions

- **Asset tree**: the equipment hierarchy of a facility (site, area, system, equipment, component), with each node linked to its history and instruments.
- **Reliability block diagram**: a model of how components combine to deliver a function. The arrangement of blocks, in series, in parallel, k-out-of-n or on standby, determines how their failures affect the function.
- **Failure propagation**: tracing how the failure of one component spreads through the structure that depends on it, to the production output affected.
- **Life data analysis**: fitting lifetime distributions such as Weibull to failure records, counting units still in service as censored observations.
- **Model Context Protocol (MCP)**: an open standard for connecting AI assistants to external systems and data sources.
